# Iteration 1 Diagnosis — D100_b base analysis

## Base system: confusion_disambiguation_memory (29/100 score)

## Root cause analysis

The base system's `_tokenize` uses `[A-Za-z0-9]+`, which extracts only ASCII tokens.
For Chinese legal text (LawBench), this means similarity between any two examples
is driven solely by shared date/number strings. Almost every pair ties at or near
Jaccard=0.0, making retrieval effectively random and the confusion-disambiguation
mechanism blind — it cannot identify which stored examples are most relevant.

## Error patterns observed in score diagnostics (71 wrong / 100)

1. Surface-form near-misses: model paraphrases the canonical label
   (e.g. "销售假冒注册商标商品" vs "销售假冒注册商标的商品";
   "非法种植罂粟" vs "非法种植毒品原植物").
2. Specificity errors: model picks a general charge when a specific one applies
   ("诈骗" vs "合同诈骗"; "行贿" vs "单位行贿").
3. Multi-charge omissions: model lists one charge when facts support two
   ("故意伤害" vs "故意伤害;故意毁坏财物").

## Iteration 1 candidates

- A (exploitation): cjk_bigram_confusion_memory — fix retrieval signal by
  replacing ASCII-only tokenizer with CJK character bigrams. Restores the
  confusion disambiguation mechanism so it actually functions over Chinese text.
- B (exploration): label_glossary_memory — accumulate canonical label strings
  during training and inject them as a reference glossary in the prompt to
  anchor the LLM to exact forms and reduce near-miss errors.

## Takeaway for future iterations

The tokenizer was the single biggest latent bug. Future iterations that build
on retrieval should keep the CJK bigram tokenizer. If glossary helps, combining
it with the confusion disambiguation mechanism is the natural next step.
